# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: What was saved is word for word what I typed, hearing aids, phone captions and my five rungs, with nothing reworded.
screens.why7: My five rungs sit on one measure, how much of the conversation was followed: the first rung is today's way working ('Followed everything that was said'), the last is outright failure ('Could not follow it at all'), the steps between are distinct, so the belief can be both supported and refuted; the second box never asks where 'good enough' ends, so the line falls to its default under the first rung, which is still a working rung.
screens.instead: How do deaf and hard-of-hearing adults keep up with a group conversation today, and with what (e.g. 'hearing aids and lipreading', 'live captions on a phone')? Then: how well did it go, best to worst, and which of those still counts as good enough?

screens.why1: Right after I said how my people follow conversations today, it makes sense to set out how that went, before the study asks strangers to grade their last time.
screens.why2: 'Followed everything', 'caught only the gist', 'missed most of it' are how deaf and hard-of-hearing people actually talk about a conversation, and I read the whole list in one pass.
screens.why3: Anyone in my segment knows exactly how much of their last group conversation they followed; it's the thing they live with every week.
screens.why4: Five distinct steps of how much was followed, from everything to nothing, with no gap and no two meaning the same; the escape belongs to the stranger's item, not this check.
screens.why5: It keeps my measure, how much of the talk they followed, and my rungs; 'join' isn't graded here, but following is the step that hurts, so the meaning holds.
screens.why7: One measure (share of the talk followed), five rungs best to worst, a working first rung and an outright failure last, the line under 'Missed only a little' so two count against the belief and three for it, and the bar names a rung that is on the list.

screens.why1: Saving my answers and settling the interviewer before strangers see the study belongs right here, after the problem checks and just before it goes out.
screens.why2: 'Save your answers' is plain, but 'lock and record the face Keel preselects' needs a second read: I'd have to work out that 'face' means the AI interviewer's on-screen face, and 'lock' and 'record' aren't words I'd use for that.
screens.why3: Deciding whether to save my own study and keep the interviewer Keel picked is my own decision to make.
screens.why4: Keeping the preselected face covers the default, but the screen doesn't show what the other choice is or how to swap the face, which matters for deaf respondents who need to see a face clearly or would rather have captions only.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my wording of the wearer, the job or the circumstance; it only saves what I already confirmed.
screens.instead: Save your answers -- options: 'Save and use the interviewer Keel picked' / 'Save and choose a different interviewer face' / 'Save with captions-only, no face'

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will take the study is the natural last step after saving my answers, before I send the link.
screens.why2: The options are plain, but the heading 'New link' doesn't say what I'm being asked to decide; I had to read the options to see it was a choice of format.
screens.why3: I know my wearers and how they take in a question, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete as formats, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents 'asks each question aloud' and 'speak into it' are odd unless the screen says the interviewer is captioned, and nothing does.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks here, and my pick of Read and tap is kept as I made it.
screens.instead: How should people take your study? Read and tap (they read each question and tap or type) / AI interviewer (a face on video asks each question, shown with captions; they answer by typing, tapping or talking) / Let them choose.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is plain, but the number beside it, a median of 4 days out of 7, sits inside my 4-to-7 range, so it reads like a pass; the number that actually decides the split (4 of 7 against a bar of 5, one short) is only down on the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives what was counted, over 7, and where the bar sits, but the Frequency line packs median, below, at-or-beyond, bar and shortfall into one run, and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I read both twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency, Importance and Current solution carry my actor, my 7-day window and my job, 'follow what hearing people are saying', in words I recognise as mine.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page tells me what a frequency split means for AirCaps: whether to narrow to the heavy-week wearers, re-ask, or move on to the solution stage; 'What it measures' only explains the scoring.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but three beliefs about all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults ('at least 8 in 10') are called 'Holding up' on 7 people with no word that 7 is few, and the statement's '20% at best' reads as a finding when it is my co-founder's own quote.
screens.instead: People disagree on how often: 4 of 7 lose the thread 4 or more days a week, one short of your bar of 5; every one of them did lose it this week, and with only 7 answers, ask a few more how many days before you size the market on daily use.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with my bar marked at 6, labelled as at least 8 in 10, so what is counted, out of how many, and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Prevalence and keeps my band and window, but the belief line drops my segment's qualifiers ('in the US who talk with hearing people every week'), and the Asked line carries a stray 'the most recent time it happened' that belongs to the story prompt, not the gate.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me where to look, but not what this means for AirCaps: that whether people have the problem isn't my risk, and how often it happens (already 'People disagree' on the stage page) is.
screens.why_b5: n is visible as 7 answered and 7 counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and 'common among these 7' keeps the claim to the people who answered.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost track of such a conversation in the last 7 days: all 7 said yes, above your bar of 6, though 7 is a lean. Having the problem isn't your risk; how often it happens is, so read Frequency next.

screens.why_b1: People disagree sits beside 4 of 7 at or above my low against a bar of 5 of 7, one short, so I know the verdict and the number behind it, though the verdict line says the 4 and 3 split three times over.
screens.why_b2: The strip (4 for, 3 against, marker at 5) reads at once, but the chart runs from 0 when no one could answer 0, gives no per-day counts in words, and the legend's 'what you said' next to 'at what you said' took me a second look to tell apart.
screens.why_b3: Frequency on 4 to 7 days out of 7, losing track of a conversation with hearing people, is my belief in my own clause, even though 'face-to-face' from my job line is not there.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me on without saying what this split means for my wedge, for example that three of the seven lose the thread only a few days a week, so heavy daily wear may not be everyone's pattern.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen calls it 'a lean, not a call', but tagging the question 'the most recent time it happened' misdescribes a count over 7 days, and the per-person rows give no day counts, so I can't check how far below my low the three sit.
screens.instead: Show each person's day count (e.g. Harriet 2, Ruth 3), drop 'the most recent time it happened' and the 0 tick, and say: 4 of 7 lose the thread on 4+ days, 3 on fewer, so the near-daily wearer is real but not the whole segment; test whether the 2-to-3-day group still values the glasses.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: Who was counted and where the bar sits are clear, but the caption says "each picked two" while the bars total 13, not 14, so I had to look twice to work out that one person stopped at Nothing else.
screens.why_b3: The belief line uses my actor, my circumstance and the four rows, and "Following what hearing people are saying" is my problem in my words, though it sits close to the job itself.
screens.why_b4: The So line rightly says this shows top two, not first place, but it doesn't tell me what that means for the glasses, such as leading with following the talk over getting a word in.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, the screen calls the group "a lean, not a call", and it explicitly declines to claim the problem ranks first.
screens.instead: Say "7 people · up to two picks each · 13 picks (one stopped after this one)", and add: "Following the talk beats getting a word in (3) for all 7, so lead with captions for following and treat joining in as second."

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits with '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see the result and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The five rungs show their counts (0/1/3/3/0, which add to 7), the line sits under 'Missed only a little', and the strip marks my bar at 5 against 6 for, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Current solution is my dimension, but the belief's act became 'following what hearing people said in a conversation', which drops the 'join' and 'face-to-face' of my job; it is still recognisable as my belief.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is true but could close any card; it doesn't say the glasses now have to beat 'caught only the gist' for the people who lost most of it.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible throughout, the count line calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the one person against is shown with his own reason (the end seat on his good side), so nothing claims more than seven people carry.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, and none followed everything; next, test whether the glasses move people from 'caught only the gist' up to 'missed only a little' in group conversations.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see the result and the count that decides it together.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Current solution, and the belief line is my circumstance in my words: deaf and hard-of-hearing adults still can't follow what hearing people say in a conversation.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what the result means for the idea, and the Frequency split (the one line that didn't hold, which made the stage 'People disagree') gets only 'a number has no why worth a question', so I don't know what to do about it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and 6 of 7 isn't oversold, but the header 'When a line fails' sits over a line that held, which suggests something failed here.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's quote is about single-sided deafness handled by taking the end seat with everyone on his good side, which shows me a sub-segment that manages without captions, something I hadn't separated out.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7. The one holdout is deaf on one side and manages by choosing his seat, so unilateral loss may be a weaker wedge. Frequency split 4 to 3 below your 4 to 7 days: consider whether the wedge is weekly group settings rather than daily use.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it's obvious why they would check that I talk with hearing people every week before asking anything else.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and other deaf people actually talk about the people around us, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I talk with in a week (people at work, the shop, my family), so I don't have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a gate question and nothing is missing, though "talk" leaves open whether texting or emailing a hearing person counts, when the study seems to be about face-to-face conversation.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company comes through, and the wording keeps the founder's segment of hearing people every week.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to answer, but "I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No." is clumsy for a yes-or-no question where just "Yes or no" would do, and a spoken-only version is no use to someone like me who can't hear it without captions.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost the thread with them this week.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of a conversation' is exactly how I'd put it; I'd answer it on one hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I got lost at the dinner table or the shop counter this week; it's my own life.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips sit with the story box after a Yes, not the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'face-to-face' was dropped, so a phone or video call where I lost the thread could also get a Yes.
screens.why6: One short question with 'Yes or no' at the end; easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It asks about the hurt, losing the thread, not the everyday act of talking with hearing people, so someone with a quiet week or good captions can truly say No; two answers and no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to losing track of a conversation this week, asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of a conversation with hearing people' is how I'd say it myself, and counting days in the last week is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I missed what was being said at work, at the shop or with family, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer with no overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the one way out.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me; the words are the ones people like me use.
screens.why6: It is one short question, then 'say a number from 1 to 7' and the escape, which is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the 7-day window, from 1 to 7 with no 0, the unit is said once in the window phrase, the event is a single act, and 'I can't recall' is the only escape.

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I lost track of a conversation, it makes sense to ask which hard part of talking with hearing people I would most want made easier.
screens.why2: Every row is something I would say myself about talking with hearing people, so I can answer on the first read.
screens.why3: I live all four of these every week at work, at the shop and at family dinners, so I can answer from my last conversation without guessing.
screens.why4: Laughing along when the joke has passed is really part of not following what people are saying, so it overlaps the following row, while the other rows stand apart and None of these fits.
screens.why5: The earlier screens were about losing track when talk is fast or noisy, but the own row has become the plain job of following what people say, so it has drifted a little from that moment.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four spoken phrases I can hold, and only the joke row runs a little long.
screens.why7: The own item is present, not first, with three other rows and None of these at the first ask, so the belief can be supported or refuted; but the own row restates the job rather than the part that goes wrong when talk is too fast or noisy, and the joke row is a piece of it.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up when everyone talks fast or over noise · Getting a word in at the right moment · Turning round when someone speaks from behind · Asking people to repeat without holding things up · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lose track and what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how my last conversation actually went for me.
screens.why2: I understand it, but 'your last conversation' and then 'in a conversation' says it twice, and dropping 'with hearing people' up front made me read it again to be sure it meant the hearing ones.
screens.why3: I know exactly how much I caught at my last conversation with hearing people; that's my every day.
screens.why4: The five are my words and run from all to nothing, but 'caught only the gist' and 'missed most of it' overlap for me, since getting the gist usually means I missed most of the detail.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan comes through; it's just about me following people.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list I can hold, but the stem is a mouthful with 'conversation' twice in one breath.
screens.why7: One measure (how much I followed) from a working first rung to failing outright in five parallel steps, and 'I can't recall' is the right escape since nobody else can follow a conversation for me.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed everything that was said; missed only a little; got the gist but missed details; missed most of it; or could not follow it at all. Or say you can't recall.

typo_leaks.text: How far back should deaf or hard-of-hearing aduts look for the last time a conversation with hearingg people is too fast or too noisy to follow?
